annotations.text:
ABSTRACT
Continual learning with large language models faces the challenge of catastrophic forgetting, where adapting to new tasks degrades performance on previously learned ones. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enables efficient fine-tuning but still suffers from forgetting in sequential learning settings. Recent SVDbased initialization methods for LoRA, such as PiSSA (top singular components) and MiLoRA (bottom components), represent endpoint choices on the singular spectrum. We propose MidPC, which initializes LoRA adapters from intermediate singular components, hypothesizing that the middle spectral region offers a better stability-plasticity trade-off. On the FOREVER Standard CL benchmark with Qwen3-0.6B, MidPC achieves 84.8% overall performance and −1.7% backward transfer, significantly outperforming PiSSA (66.7%, −15.0%) and MiLoRA (81.6%, −5.0%). Spectral analysis reveals that MidPC maintains stable subspace alignment while achieving moderate spectral imbalance. Learning rate matching experiments confirm this is a genuine spectral effect, with 91.9% of the advantage over MiLoRA retained after controlling for conditioning differences.
annotations.comment:
The abstract claims to propose an intermediate SVD component initialization, implying a novel discovery. However, Quercia et al. (2026) [1] independently proposed and empirically validated that fine-tuning intermediate principal components yields better performance-forgetting trade-offs than PiSSA and MiLoRA in both NLP and computer vision continual learning settings. The abstract currently lacks any acknowledgment of this substantially overlapping prior work. To defend the paper's contribution, explicitly differentiate MidPC from Quercia et al. (2026)—for instance, by highlighting unique spectral diagnostics, the specific FOREVER benchmark application, or distinct slice-selection protocols—and bound the novelty claim to avoid being classified as a substantially overlapped result.

Mentor Revised Version: "Continual learning with large language models faces the challenge of catastrophic forgetting... Recent SVD-based initialization methods for LoRA, such as PiSSA and MiLoRA, represent endpoint choices on the singular spectrum. While recent work has begun exploring intermediate components [1], the specific stability-plasticity dynamics under sequential LLM adaptation remain under-analyzed. We propose MidPC..."

annotations.summary: Abstract lacks acknowledgment of Quercia et al. (2026), which directly proposes intermediate SVD slice initialization for continual learning, threatening the core novelty claim.

annotations.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2021) has emerged as a leading approach for efficient finetuning, introducing trainable low-rank matrices while keeping pretrained weights frozen. However, standard LoRA still suffers from forgetting in continual learning settings (Liang & Li, 2024). Recent work has explored SVD-based initialization strategies to address this: PiSSA (Meng et al., 2024) initializes adapters from top singular components for faster convergence, while MiLoRA (Wang et al., 2024) uses bottom components to preserve pretrained knowledge. Yet these approaches represent endpoint choices on the singular spectrum, leaving the intermediate region unexplored.
annotations.comment:
The narrative establishes the problem of catastrophic forgetting in LLMs and transitions to LoRA-based adaptation. This is well-motivated and follows a clear problem-to-solution arc. However, the paragraph does not clearly articulate *why* SVD-based initialization specifically matters for continual learning; it only mentions that standard LoRA "suffers from forgetting."

To strengthen this paragraph, add one sentence connecting the spectral properties of pretrained weights to the stability-plasticity dilemma—e.g., explaining that high-variance directions encode shared knowledge across tasks, making their selection critical for interference control.

Mentor Revised Version: "Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2021) has emerged as a leading approach for efficient fine-tuning, introducing trainable low-rank matrices while keeping pretrained weights frozen. However, standard LoRA still suffers from forgetting in continual learning settings (Liang & Li, 2024). The choice of *which* directions to adapt matters: high-variance directions encode knowledge shared across tasks, while low-variance directions may be less stable under optimization. Recent work has explored SVD-based initialization strategies to address this: PiSSA (Meng et al., 2024) initializes adapters from top singular components for faster convergence, while MiLoRA (Wang et al., 2024) uses bottom components to preserve pretrained knowledge."
annotations.summary: Introduction paragraph introduces SVD-based methods but lacks explicit link between spectral direction selection and stability-plasticity trade-off.

annotations.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2021) has emerged as a leading approach for efficient finetuning, introducing trainable low-rank matrices while keeping pretrained weights frozen. However, standard LoRA still suffers from forgetting in continual learning settings (Liang & Li, 2024). Recent work has explored SVD-based initialization strategies to address this: PiSSA (Meng et al., 2024) initializes adapters from top singular components for faster convergence, while MiLoRA (Wang et al., 2024) uses bottom components to preserve pretrained knowledge. Yet these approaches represent endpoint choices on the singular spectrum, leaving the intermediate region unexplored.
annotations.comment:
This paragraph claims that "the intermediate region [is] unexplored." This statement is factually incorrect given the recent work of Quercia et al. (2026) [1], which explicitly proposes and validates intermediate SVD slice initialization for continual learning, demonstrating a U-shaped forgetting curve where intermediate components outperform both PiSSA (top) and MiLoRA (bottom). This claim of unexplored territory directly contradicts established literature and undermines the novelty case.

Replace the claim with a bounded statement acknowledging prior work while positioning MidPC's specific differentiators (e.g., spectral diagnostics, learning rate matching analysis, or FOREVER benchmark evaluation).

Mentor Revised Version: "Yet these approaches represent endpoint choices on the singular spectrum. While recent work has begun exploring intermediate spectral regions [1], the specific stability-plasticity dynamics of middle slices under sequential LLM adaptation—and their robustness to task-order variations—remain under-characterized."

References:
[1] Least but not Last: Fine-tuning Intermediate Principal Components for Better Performance-Forgetting Trade-Offs 2602.03493
annotations.summary: Claim that intermediate region is "unexplored" directly contradicts Quercia et al. (2026), which explicitly proposes intermediate SVD slice initialization for continual learning.

annotations.text: Our contributions are threefold. First, we propose MidPC, a simple SVD-slice initialization strategy that selects intermediate singular components for LoRA adapters in continual learning. Second, we demonstrate that MidPC achieves state-of-the-art performance among SVD-based methods, reducing forgetting by 13.3 percentage points compared to PiSSA and 3.3 percentage points compared to MiLoRA. Third, we provide spectral analysis showing that MidPC maintains stable subspace alignment while achieving moderate spectral imbalance, and verify through learning rate matching that the improvement reflects a genuine spectral effect, with 91.9% of the advantage over MiLoRA retained after controlling for conditioning differences.
annotations.comment:
The contributions paragraph states "MidPC achieves state-of-the-art performance among SVD-based methods." This claim is problematic for two reasons. First, Quercia et al. (2026) [1] also demonstrates that intermediate SVD slices outperform PiSSA and MiLoRA in continual learning settings, so "state-of-the-art among SVD-based methods" is not uniquely MidPC's. Second, the comparison is limited to two baselines (PiSSA and MiLoRA) on one benchmark (FOREVER Standard CL) with one model (Qwen3-0.6B). Broader SVD-based methods like SC-LoRA [2], GOAT [3], and LoRA-DA [4] address knowledge preservation but use different subspace construction strategies; direct comparison is not provided.

Bound the claim to the specific evaluation setting and acknowledge Quercia et al. (2026). Specify what differentiates MidPC's empirical contribution.

Mentor Revised Version: "Second, we demonstrate that MidPC outperforms PiSSA and MiLoRA on the FOREVER Standard CL benchmark with Qwen3-0.6B, reducing forgetting by 13.3 percentage points compared to PiSSA and 3.3 percentage points compared to MiLoRA. We position these results relative to recent intermediate-component findings [1] and highlight our spectral diagnostics as a differentiating contribution."

References:
[1] Least but not Last: Fine-tuning Intermediate Principal Components for Better Performance-Forgetting Trade-Offs 2602.03493

[2] SC-LoRA: Balancing Efficient Fine-tuning and Knowledge Preservation via Subspace-Constrained LoRA 2505.23724

[3] Make LoRA Great Again: Boosting LoRA with Adaptive Singular Values and Mixture-of-Experts Optimization Alignment 2502.16894

[4] LoRA-DA: Data-Aware Initialization for Low-Rank Adaptation via Asymptotic Analysis 2510.24561
annotations.summary: "State-of-the-art among SVD-based methods" overclaim: Quercia et al. (2026) shows similar intermediate-component gains; comparison scope is limited to one benchmark/model.

annotations.text: SVD-based Initialization. Recent work has revealed that the initialization of LoRA adapters significantly impacts both learning efficiency and knowledge preservation. PiSSA (Meng et al., 2024) initializes adapters from the principal (top) singular components of pretrained weights, achieving faster convergence by leveraging high-variance directions. Conversely, MiLoRA (Wang et al., 2024) uses minor (bottom) singular components, arguing that adapting less important directions better preserves pretrained knowledge. Gu et al. (2026) provide theoretical analysis showing that spectral imbalance in LoRA updates contributes to forgetting in continual learning. Shuttleworth et al. (2024) further demonstrate fundamental differences between LoRA and full fine-tuning in terms of spectral properties. These findings motivate our investigation of intermediate spectral regions, which may offer a better balance between learning capacity and stability.
annotations.comment:
The SVD-based Initialization related-work paragraph covers PiSSA, MiLoRA, Gu et al. (2026), and Shuttleworth et al. (2024) but omits Quercia et al. (2026) [1], which is the most directly relevant prior work: it explicitly proposes intermediate principal component initialization for LoRA and validates it on continual learning settings. Also missing are SC-LoRA [2] (subspace-constrained LoRA for knowledge preservation) and "Learning Rate Matters" [3], which shows that learning rate tuning can eliminate performance gaps between SVD-based methods and vanilla LoRA—directly relevant to the manuscript's learning rate matching analysis.\n\nAdding these references is essential for a credible novelty position and for contextualizing the learning rate matching findings.\n\nMentor Revised Version: "SVD-based Initialization. Recent work has revealed that the initialization of LoRA adapters significantly impacts both learning efficiency and knowledge preservation. PiSSA (Meng et al., 2024) initializes adapters from the principal (top) singular components... MiLoRA (Wang et al., 2024) uses minor (bottom) singular components... Quercia et al. (2026) [1] further demonstrate that intermediate principal components can outperform both endpoints in continual learning settings. Gu et al. (2026) provide theoretical analysis showing that spectral imbalance contributes to forgetting... Lee et al. (2026) [3] show that learning rate sensitivity across SVD-based methods can account for much of their reported performance differences."

References:
[1] Least but not Last: Fine-tuning Intermediate Principal Components for Better Performance-Forgetting Trade-Offs 2602.03493

[2] SC-LoRA: Balancing Efficient Fine-tuning and Knowledge Preservation via Subspace-Constrained LoRA 2505.23724

[3] Learning Rate Matters: Vanilla LoRA May Suffice for LLM Fine-tuning 2602.04998
annotations.summary: Related Work omits Quercia et al. (2026), the most directly relevant intermediate-component paper, and Lee et al. (2026), which challenges SVD method advantages via learning rate tuning.

annotations.text:
The choice of which singular components to adapt has significant implications for continual learning. Top singular components (PiSSA) capture high-variance directions that are heavily utilized by the pretrained model. While adapting these directions enables rapid learning, it risks damaging representations shared across tasks, potentially leading to severe forgetting during sequential training. Bottom singular components (MiLoRA) represent less-optimized directions that may be safer to modify. However, these poorly-conditioned directions can become unstable under continual adaptation, potentially drifting into misaligned high-energy directions that interfere with pretrained knowledge (Shuttleworth et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2026).
We hypothesize that intermediate singular components offer a better stability-plasticity trade-off: they have sufficient variance for effective learning while avoiding the extreme sensitivity of endpoint choices.
annotations.comment:
The motivation paragraph provides an intuitive explanation for why intermediate components might be beneficial, citing Shuttleworth et al. (2024) and Gu et al. (2026). The reasoning is logically sound: top components risk damaging shared knowledge, bottom components are poorly conditioned. However, this hypothesis is now also the central claim of Quercia et al. (2026) [1], which empirically demonstrates a U-shaped forgetting curve across principal components.

To differentiate this manuscript, consider adding one sentence that frames *why* the intermediate region's benefit has not been fully characterized—for instance, noting that prior work on intermediate components lacks systematic spectral diagnostics or learning-rate-matched controls.

Mentor Revised Version: "We hypothesize that intermediate singular components offer a better stability-plasticity trade-off: they have sufficient variance for effective learning while avoiding the extreme sensitivity of endpoint choices. Recent empirical findings [1] support this intuition, but the precise spectral dynamics and conditioning effects of middle slices remain under-analyzed, particularly under learning-rate-controlled settings."

References:
[1] Least but not Last: Fine-tuning Intermediate Principal Components for Better Performance-Forgetting Trade-Offs 2602.03493
annotations.summary: Motivation is sound but overlaps with Quercia et al. (2026); add differentiating framing about spectral diagnostics and conditioning controls.

annotations.text:
The frozen base weight is set to the residual: $W _ { p } = W - \Delta W _ { s }$ . We initialize the LoRA factors to preserve the original model behavior at initialization:
$$
A = \sqrt {\frac {r}{\alpha}} \Sigma_ {s: s + r} ^ {1 / 2} V _ {s: s + r} ^ {\top}, \quad B = \sqrt {\frac {r}{\alpha}} U _ {s: s + r} \Sigma_ {s: s + r} ^ {1 / 2}\tag{2}
$$
This ensures $\begin{array} { r } { W _ { p } + \frac { \alpha } { r } B A = W } \end{array}$ , making the initialization function-preserving. Any performance differences must arise from training dynamics rather than initialization artifacts.
MidPC unifies existing approaches as special cases: PiSSA corresponds to $s ~ = ~ 0$ (top slice), MiLoRA corresponds to $s = r _ { \mathrm { m a x } } - r$ (bottom slice), and MidPC uses $s = \lfloor r _ { \operatorname* { m a x } } / 2 \rfloor$ (middle slice), where $r _ { \operatorname* { m a x } } = \operatorname* { m i n } ( m , n )$ . Figure 1 illustrates this unified framework.
annotations.comment:
The method formulation is mathematically consistent with the PiSSA/MiLoRA family of SVD-based LoRA initializations. Equation (1) correctly defines the SVD slice, and Equation (2) provides the correct factorization to ensure function-preserving initialization ($W_p + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA = W$). The notation is clear, and the unification of PiSSA ($s=0$), MiLoRA ($s=r_{max}-r$), and MidPC ($s=\lfloor r_{max}/2 \rfloor$) as special cases is elegant.

One minor issue: the manuscript uses $\frac{\alpha}{r}$ in the function-preserving check (Eq. 2) but $\frac{\alpha}{n}$ in the standard LoRA definition (Section 3.1). This is intentional (PiSSA-style scaling), but the difference should be explicitly stated to avoid confusion. Authors should add one sentence noting the scaling convention change from standard LoRA to SVD-based initialization.

Mentor Revised Version: "The frozen base weight is set to the residual: $W_p = W - \Delta W_s$. We initialize the LoRA factors to preserve the original model behavior at initialization:
$$A = \sqrt{\frac{r}{\alpha}} \Sigma_{s:s+r}^{1/2} V_{s:s+r}^\top, \quad B = \sqrt{\frac{r}{\alpha}} U_{s:s+r} \Sigma_{s:s+r}^{1/2}$$
This ensures $W_p + \frac{\alpha}{r} BA = W$, making the initialization function-preserving. Note that we adopt the PiSSA-style scaling $\alpha/r$ rather than the standard LoRA scaling $\alpha/n$, which is standard practice for SVD-based initialization methods to match singular value magnitudes."
annotations.summary: Method formulas are mathematically correct; clarify the scaling convention difference ($\alpha/r$ vs $\alpha/n$) between SVD-based methods and standard LoRA.

annotations.text: Table 1 presents the main results. MidPC achieves the best overall performance with OP=84.8% and BWT=−1.7%, significantly outperforming both endpoint SVD-slice methods. Compared to PiSSA (top slice), MidPC improves OP by 18.1 percentage points and reduces forgetting by 13.3 percentage points. Compared to MiLoRA (bottom slice), MidPC improves OP by 3.2 percentage points and reduces forgetting by 3.3 percentage points. The improvements are statistically significant $( p \ <$ 0.01 vs PiSSA, $p < 0 . 0 5$ vs MiLoRA). Notably, PiSSA exhibits severe forgetting (BWT=−15.0%)
annotations.comment:
The main results paragraph reports statistical significance claims: "p < 0.01 vs PiSSA, p < 0.05 vs MiLoRA." However, the experimental setup specifies only 6 total runs per method (2 task orders × 3 random seeds). With such a small sample size, computing reliable p-values is problematic: standard parametric tests (t-test) require assumptions about normality that cannot be verified with n=6, and the effective degrees of freedom are extremely limited. Furthermore, the manuscript does not specify which statistical test was used, whether the tests were paired or unpaired, or how task-order variance was accounted for in the significance testing.

To make these claims defensible, either: (1) increase the number of random seeds to at least 5-10 to provide adequate statistical power, or (2) downgrade the language to report effect sizes and standard deviations without formal p-value claims, or (3) explicitly state the statistical test used and justify its validity under n=6.

Mentor Revised Version: "The improvements over PiSSA and MiLoRA are consistent across both task orders and all seeds. With the limited number of runs (6 per method), we report mean±std and effect sizes rather than formal significance tests, noting that the large delta vs PiSSA (OP +18.1pp, BWT +13.3pp) is robust while the smaller delta vs MiLoRA (OP +3.2pp, BWT +3.3pp) warrants further validation with additional seeds."
annotations.summary: p-value significance claims with only 6 total runs per method lack statistical power and test specification; downgrade claims or increase seeds.

annotations.text:
4.4 LEARNING RATE MATCHING ANALYSIS
Different SVD slices have different singular value magnitudes, which could affect effective learning rates and confound our conclusions. To address this, we conducted a learning rate matching experiment where we adjusted the learning rates of PiSSA and MiLoRA to match MidPC’s earlystep update norms (Table 2). After learning rate matching, 91.9% of MidPC’s BWT advantage over MiLoRA is retained, confirming that the improvement reflects a genuine spectral effect rather than a conditioning artifact. The advantage over PiSSA is partially explained by conditioning (35.2% retained), but MidPC still maintains substantial improvement even after adjustment.
annotations.comment:
The learning rate matching analysis is a strong methodological contribution, directly addressing the confound that different SVD slices have different singular value magnitudes affecting effective learning rates. However, the interpretation "91.9% of MidPC's BWT advantage over MiLoRA is retained, confirming that the improvement reflects a genuine spectral effect" should be contextualized against Lee et al. (2026) [1], which systematically shows that learning rate tuning can eliminate performance gaps between SVD-based methods and vanilla LoRA. 

The manuscript should explicitly discuss how its learning rate matching protocol differs from or builds upon Lee et al. (2026), and acknowledge that the 35.2% retention for PiSSA suggests conditioning effects are substantial for top-slice comparisons.

Mentor Revised Version: "After learning rate matching, 91.9% of MidPC's BWT advantage over MiLoRA is retained, suggesting the improvement reflects a genuine spectral effect rather than a conditioning artifact alone. This finding aligns with and extends the learning-rate-sensitivity analysis of Lee et al. (2026) [1], which demonstrated that SVD-based methods favor distinct learning rate ranges. Notably, the advantage over PiSSA is partially explained by conditioning (35.2% retained), indicating that top-slice comparisons are more sensitive to learning rate effects than bottom-slice comparisons."

References:
[1] Learning Rate Matters: Vanilla LoRA May Suffice for LLM Fine-tuning 2602.04998
annotations.summary: Learning rate matching analysis is strong; should contextualize findings against Lee et al. (2026) on SVD method learning rate sensitivity.

annotations.text:
4.5 ROBUSTNESS ACROSS TASK ORDERS
Table 3 shows that MidPC demonstrates consistent performance across different task orderings. MidPC achieves the best OP and BWT in both orders, with remarkably stable BWT (−1.7%) regardless of task sequence. In contrast, MiLoRA shows more variance between orders (BWT ranges from −7.2% to −2.8%), and PiSSA exhibits high variability with severe forgetting in Order 2 (BWT=−17.2%). This robustness suggests that intermediate SVD slices provide a more reliable stability-plasticity trade-off across different continual learning scenarios.
annotations.comment:
The robustness paragraph provides a useful analysis of task-order sensitivity, showing that MidPC maintains stable BWT (−1.7%) across both orders while PiSSA and MiLoRA show higher variance. This is an important finding that supports the stability claim of intermediate slices.

However, only two task orders are tested, which limits the generalizability of the robustness claim. The phrase "remarkably stable BWT" is reasonable given the data, but readers should understand that this is validated over only 2 orderings.

Mentor Revised Version: "Table 3 shows that MidPC demonstrates consistent performance across the two evaluated task orderings. MidPC achieves the best OP and BWT in both orders, with stable BWT (−1.7%) regardless of task sequence. In contrast, MiLoRA shows more variance between orders (BWT ranges from −7.2% to −2.8%), and PiSSA exhibits high variability with severe forgetting in Order 2 (BWT=−17.2%). While tested over only two orderings, this robustness is consistent with intermediate SVD slices providing a more reliable stability-plasticity trade-off."
annotations.summary: Task-order robustness is a valuable finding but validated over only 2 orderings; bound claim scope accordingly.

annotations.text:
5 CONCLUSION
We presented MidPC, a simple yet effective approach for continual learning with LoRA that initializes adapters from intermediate singular components rather than endpoint choices. On the FOR-EVER Standard CL benchmark, MidPC achieves 84.8% overall performance and −1.7% backward transfer, substantially outperforming both PiSSA and MiLoRA. Spectral analysis reveals that intermediate slices maintain stable subspace alignment while achieving moderate spectral imbalance, providing a favorable stability-plasticity trade-off. Our learning rate matching experiments confirm this is a genuine spectral effect rather than a conditioning artifact. While our evaluation is limited to one model and benchmark, MidPC offers a zero-cost initialization knob that can be combined with other continual learning techniques. Future work could explore adaptive slice selection based on task characteristics.
annotations.comment:
The conclusion accurately summarizes the paper's validated findings and honestly acknowledges limitations (one model, one benchmark). It also provides a concrete future direction (adaptive slice selection). This is well-structured.

However, the conclusion should also acknowledge Quercia et al. (2026) [1] to maintain consistency with the novelty discussion. The conclusion currently reads as if MidPC is the sole contributor to the intermediate-component insight.

Mentor Revised Version: "We presented MidPC, a simple yet effective approach for continual learning with LoRA that initializes adapters from intermediate singular components rather than endpoint choices. Building on recent evidence that intermediate components offer favorable trade-offs [1], we provide spectral diagnostics and learning rate matching analysis that characterize the conditioning effects differentiating middle slices from endpoints. On the FOREVER Standard CL benchmark, MidPC achieves 84.8% overall performance and −1.7% backward transfer... While our evaluation is limited to one model and benchmark, MidPC offers a zero-cost initialization knob..."

References:
[1] Least but not Last: Fine-tuning Intermediate Principal Components for Better Performance-Forgetting Trade-Offs 2602.03493
annotations.summary: Conclusion should acknowledge Quercia et al. (2026) to maintain consistency with novelty discussion and position MidPC's differentiating contributions.
